appraisal_events.evidence: Charlus rails that his family's former estate now belongs to 'ces Israël,' whom he claims are not even entitled to a proper name, and jokes that destroying Lenôtre's park should send them to prison, adding 'il y a sans doute tant d'autres choses pour lesquelles ils devraient y être!'
appraisal_events.explanation: Charlus loudly discredits the family that bought his ancestral home, though the narrator's mid-speech image of Charlus furtively hiding an indecent handkerchief undercuts the moral authority behind his contempt.

appraisal_events.evidence: Charlus knocks at the narrator's bedroom door at night to personally bring him a Bergotte book, 'pour vous aider à passer ces moments où vous ne vous sentez pas heureux.'
appraisal_events.explanation: Despite his dry tone, Charlus singles out the narrator for private, personal kindness, crossing from public salon distance into his own bedroom to offer comfort.

status_effects.explanation: Charlus denies the family even a proper name and casts their taste and standing as worthless, even prison-worthy.
The narrator's inserted image of Charlus furtively hiding a telltale handkerchief mid-tirade undercuts his self-righteous moralizing, hinting at hypocrisy behind his loud contempt.
The narrator receives unexpected personal solicitude and comfort from an intimidating aristocrat, easing his private unhappiness.
Charlus crosses the threshold into the narrator's private bedroom to extend personal attention, marking him singled out rather than kept at the usual social distance.

ambiguities: The narrator's stance toward Charlus's tirade against the Israël family is layered: the mid-speech handkerchief detail may ironize Charlus's self-righteousness without directly endorsing or condemning his view of the family.
